Well, thank you for seeing me. I, um... I guess I'm here because I just really don't feel like myself anymore. It's hard to explain, but what finally brought me in is this... this total shift in how I spend my time. 

I've always been a very active person, you know? Between my job—I'm a teaching assistant, and working with kids takes a lot of energy—but I always, always made a point to make time for my own things. I used to do a lot of painting, mostly watercolors, just little landscapes and things, but I loved it. And I'd go hiking on the weekends when the weather was nice. I've also been in a choir for years, and I never, ever missed our Sunday family gatherings. I was usually the one coordinating who brings what dish for those. 

But lately... I don't know, it's like a switch flipped. Now, even when I have a free hour, like on a Saturday afternoon where I'd normally be setting up my easel or calling my sister to go for a walk, I just... I just sit there. I sit in the living room or at the kitchen table and I am just completely unable to care about any of it. I look at my paints and I feel absolutely nothing. I think about choir practice and I just don't have the desire to go at all. It's just so frustrating because I know I used to love those things, but now I just sit there letting the time pass, and it's been going on long enough that I figured I needed to talk to a doctor about it, because it's just so completely unlike me...

Well, it hasn't just been a sudden thing, like waking up one morning and feeling this way. It's... it's been building up, really. I'd say it's been about eight months now. I can actually pinpoint it pretty well because it started right around the time I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative at school. 

I remember when they first asked me to lead it, I was actually excited. It sounded like exactly the kind of project I'd normally throw myself into, finding ways to integrate creative arts into the science and math programs for the kids. I spent the first few weeks gathering materials, looking up project ideas... but then, it just started to feel so heavy. And it wasn't just the work. I thought maybe I was just tired from the extra responsibility, but then it started bleeding into my weekends. First, I stopped going to choir, telling myself I just needed Sunday mornings to rest. Then the paints stayed in the drawer. 

And now, eight months later, here I am, not doing any of it. It's like the color just drained out of everything, slowly, day by day, since that curriculum project started. I keep thinking, 'Oh, when this term is over, I'll get back to normal,' or 'When I finish this next lesson plan, I'll have energy for hiking again.' But the term ends, the plans are done, and I still just... sit there. It's been eight whole months of just... sitting there.

Well, it's not exactly neutral, and it's definitely not just flat... I mean, I wish it were just flat, because that sounds almost peaceful, doesn't it? But it's more like... it's like this heavy, suffocating feeling that just settles over me from the moment I wake up. Most days, I feel like there's this thick, heavy gray film covering absolutely everything. I can literally be standing right in the middle of a bustling classroom, surrounded by twenty-five energetic kids working on a science project, or I can be sitting at my own kitchen table having dinner with my husband, Mark—we've been married for twenty years, and he's usually so good at making me laugh—and despite all of that, despite being surrounded by people, I just feel completely hollow inside. 

And it's not just a passing feeling, it's this constant, lingering ache. I'll be in the middle of explaining a math concept to a student, and suddenly I just feel so incredibly close to tears for absolutely no reason at all. I have to physically bite the inside of my cheek or dig my nails into my palm just to keep from crying right there in front of the chalkboard. And it happens nearly every single day. I wake up, and that gray film is there, and it stays with me through the morning announcements, through lunch duty, through the drive home, through dinner... it just never lifts. It's so exhausting feeling this deeply sad all the time, especially when I look around and know I have a good life, a good job, a good husband. But the hollowness is just... it's just always there, pressing down on me, making everything feel so incredibly difficult to get through.

Well, um... I haven't really noticed any major changes with those specific things, to be honest. I mean, as far as my energy goes, like I said before, everything just feels so heavy and difficult, like I'm moving through molasses, but it's not like I'm physically exhausted in the way you'd be after running a marathon, you know? I've also been in a choir for years, and I never, ever missed our Sunday family gatherings. I was usually the one coordinating who brings what dish for those. \n\nBut lately... I don't know, it's like a switch flipped. Now, even when I have a free hour, like on a Saturday afternoon where I'd normally be setting up my easel or calling my sister to go for a walk, I just... I just sit there. I sit in the living room or at the kitchen table and I am just completely unable to care about any of it. I look at my paints and I feel absolutely nothing. I think about choir practice and I just don't have the desire to go at all. It's just so frustrating because I know I used to love those things, but now I just sit there letting the time pass, and it's been going on long enough that I figured I needed to talk to a doctor about it, because it's just so completely unlike me...\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me how long this lack of interest or motivation has been going on?\n\nPatient: Well, it hasn't just been a sudden thing, like waking up one morning and feeling this way. It's... it's been building up, really. I'd say it's been about eight months now. I can actually pinpoint it pretty well because it started right around the time I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative at school. \n\nI remember when they first asked me to lead it, I was actually excited. It sounded like exactly the kind of project I'd normally throw myself into, finding ways to integrate creative arts into the science and math programs for the kids. I spent the first few weeks gathering materials, looking up project ideas... but then, it just started to feel so heavy. And it wasn't just the work. I thought maybe I was just tired from the extra responsibility, but then it started bleeding into my weekends. First, I stopped going to choir, telling myself I just needed Sunday mornings to rest. Then the paints stayed in the drawer. \n\nAnd now, eight months later, here I am, not doing any of it. It's like the color just drained out of everything, slowly, day by day, since that curriculum project started. I keep thinking, 'Oh, when this term is over, I'll get back to normal,' or 'When I finish this next lesson plan, I'll have energy for hiking again.' But the term ends, the plans are done, and I still just... sit there. It's been eight whole months of just... sitting there.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed that activities you used to enjoy, like painting or hiking, no longer give you any pleasure or satisfaction?\n\nPatient: I mean... I'm not really sure how to answer that, to be perfectly honest. Because to know if they still give me pleasure or satisfaction, I feel like I would actually have to do them, right? And I just... I haven't. I haven't even tried in so long. \n\nLike, I remember a couple of weekends ago, it was a gorgeous Saturday, just perfectly clear. The light coming through my kitchen window was exactly the kind of light I used to love trying to capture. I actually went and got my watercolor pad out of the drawer. I set it on the table, and I opened my palette—it's this really lovely professional set with these deep, rich pigments that I saved up for a while back—and I just stood there staring at it. I kept thinking, 'If I just wet the brush, if I just put down one wash of blue, maybe I'll feel that little spark.' You know that feeling? When the color hits the wet paper and just blooms? I used to absolutely love that. It was always so satisfying to watch. \n\nBut standing there... I didn't feel any anticipation at all. I didn't feel a desire to see the color. I just felt completely blank. So I put it all back in the drawer. I didn't paint a single stroke. So I don't really know if the actual act of painting would feel good if I somehow forced myself to sit down and finish a whole piece, because I just can't even bring myself to start. \n\nIt's the exact same thing with my hiking boots. They're just sitting there in the mudroom, and looking at them doesn't make me want to go outside, but it doesn't make me sad either. It's just... nothing. The idea of even tying the laces feels like climbing a mountain before I even get to the trail. So I really couldn't tell you if the hike itself would be enjoyable anymore, because I just haven't been able to get out the door to find out.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, or is your mood more neutral or flat?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not exactly neutral, and it's definitely not just flat... I mean, I wish it were just flat, because that sounds almost peaceful, doesn't it? But it's more like... it's like this heavy, suffocating feeling that just settles over me from the moment I wake up. Most days, I feel like there's this thick, heavy gray film covering absolutely everything. I can literally be standing right in the middle of a bustling classroom, surrounded by twenty-five energetic kids working on a science project, or I can be sitting at my own kitchen table having dinner with my husband, Mark—we've been married for twenty years, and he's usually so good at making me laugh—and despite all of that, despite being surrounded by people, I just feel completely hollow inside. \n\nAnd it's not just a passing feeling, it's this constant, lingering ache. I'll be in the middle of explaining a math concept to a student, and suddenly I just feel so incredibly close to tears for absolutely no reason at all. I have to physically bite the inside of my cheek or dig my nails into my palm just to keep from crying right there in front of the chalkboard. And it happens nearly every single day. I wake up, and that gray film is there, and it stays with me through the morning announcements, through lunch duty, through the drive home, through dinner... it just never lifts. It's so exhausting feeling this deeply sad all the time, especially when I look around and know I have a good life, a good job, a good husband. But the hollowness is just... it's just always there, pressing down on me, making everything feel so incredibly difficult to get through.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your energy level, appetite, or ability to focus on tasks?\n\nPatient: Well, um... I haven't really noticed any major changes with those specific things, to be honest. I mean, as far as my energy goes, like I said before, everything just feels so heavy and difficult, like I'm moving through molasses, but it's not like I'm physically exhausted in the way you'd be after running a marathon, you know? It's more of a mental and emotional weight that just drags me down. I still manage to drag myself out of bed and get to school, even though it takes everything I have just to put one foot in front of the other. \n\nAnd my appetite... I think it's been pretty much the same. I still eat dinner with Mark every night. He usually cooks, bless him, because he knows I just don't have it in me right now. Last night he made this wonderful roasted chicken with root vegetables—he knows it's one of my favorites—and I ate it. I didn't really taste it, it just felt like chewing cardboard, but I ate my normal portion. I haven't gained or lost any weight that I've noticed. My clothes all still fit the same way they did at the beginning of the school year. \n\nAs for focusing... I don't know. I guess I'm still getting my work done. I still grade the papers, I still help the kids with their projects. It might take me a little longer to get through a stack of math worksheets because I find myself just staring at the red pen in my hand, wondering what the point of it all is, but I eventually get them done. I haven't made any glaring mistakes or forgotten to do anything important, at least not that anyone has pointed out to me. So, I guess... no? No real changes there, just that everything surrounding those things feels so incredibly difficult and hollow.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed that you've been moving more slowly than usual, or that you feel restless and can't sit still?\n\nPatient: I don't think so... I mean, I don't feel restless, like I need to be pacing or anything like that. And I don't think I'm actually moving any slower in a physical sense. It's funny you ask that, because just the other day I was walking down the hallway at school—it was right after second period, so the halls were completely packed with kids rushing to get to their lockers, and you know how chaotic middle schoolers can be between classes. I was carrying this huge stack of permission slips to the main office for the upcoming field trip to the science museum. Mark and I actually went to that same museum years ago, back when we were first dating, and they had this incredible exhibit on geology... but anyway, I was walking down the hall, and I realized I was keeping up with the flow of traffic just fine. I wasn't holding anyone up, I wasn't lagging behind the other teachers. \n\nBut internally? Internally, it feels like I'm moving through deep water. So to the outside world, to the kids and the principal and Mark, I probably look like I'm moving at my normal pace. I'm getting the permission slips to the office on time, I'm making dinner, I'm doing the laundry. But inside, it feels like everything has slowed to an absolute crawl. It's just that heavy, suffocating feeling again, making every action feel like a chore. But no, I haven't noticed any actual, physical slowing down, and I definitely don't feel jittery or restless. Just... heavy.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt this way before, with a prolonged period of sadness and loss of interest in activities, or is this the first time you've experienced something like this?\n\nPatient: Well, um... Even when I was deeply sad in the past, I still wanted to go out to dinner with Mark, or I still looked forward to my morning cup of coffee on the back porch, or planting my spring bulbs. But now? Now it's just that heavy gray film I told you about. So no, I have never, ever experienced anything even remotely close to this before. It's completely unprecedented for me, and honestly, it's terrifying because I just don't know how to shake it. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like myself again, the way I always did after a rough patch in the past, but... it just isn't happening this time.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period in the past where you felt down or lost interest in things for a period of at least two weeks, similar to what you’ve been experiencing now?\n\nPatient: No, no, I...
